title: Boolean retrieval (search operators and exact match)
summary: Boolean retrieval combines terms with AND, OR and NOT, and the textbook says a document either matches or does not match a query. AND tends to give high precision but low recall, OR the reverse, and a satisfactory middle ground is hard to find; on large collections the matches can far exceed what a person could read, which is why ranked retrieval exists. Google Search Help describes quotes for an exact match, a minus sign to exclude a word, and operators such as site:, before: and filetype: with no space after the colon.

items.prompt: Boolean retrieval combines terms with AND, OR and which third operator (one word, capitals)?
items.explanation: The textbook says terms are combined with the operators and, or, and not.

items.prompt: In the textbook's Boolean retrieval model, how is each document viewed?
options: A. As just a set of words
B. As a ranked list of passages
C. As a vector of weighted term scores
D. As a graph of links to other pages
items.explanation: Correct: the textbook says the model views each document as just a set of words. Wrong: ranked passages, weighted vectors and link graphs belong to other models, not the Boolean model as described.

items.prompt: True or false: Google Search Help says to put a space after an operator, as in 'site: nytimes.com'.
items.explanation: Google Search Help says not to put spaces between the operator and your search term: site:nytimes.com works, site: nytimes.com won't.

items.prompt: Why does plain Boolean matching become hard to use on a large collection?
options: A. It cannot combine terms with AND
B. Matches can far exceed what a person can read
C. It ranks every document identically by design only
D. It only works with phrases in quotes
items.explanation: Correct: the textbook says a document either matches or does not, and the number of matches can far exceed what a user could sift through. Boolean does support AND. 'Ranks identically' is not the stated problem and overstates it. Quotes for an exact match are a Google Search feature (Google Search Help: enter a word or phrase inside quotes), not a Boolean limitation.

items.prompt: A colleague says 'Joining terms with OR makes a Boolean search more precise.' Which correction fits the textbook?
options: A. OR has no effect on precision or recall
B. OR always gives the best middle ground
C. OR only works alongside proximity operators
D. OR gives low precision but high recall
items.explanation: Correct: the textbook says using OR operators gives low precision but high recall searches. Wrong: OR does change precision and recall; the textbook says a satisfactory middle ground is difficult or impossible to find; proximity operators are a separate feature.

items.prompt: Which statement is NOT supported by the textbook's section on Boolean versus ranked retrieval?
options: A. Boolean queries are precise
B. AND tends to give high precision, low recall
C. A satisfactory middle ground is easy to find
D. Many professionals prefer Boolean query models
items.explanation: Unsupported: the textbook says it is difficult or impossible to find a satisfactory middle ground. Supported: Boolean queries are precise; AND tends to produce high precision but low recall; many users, particularly professionals, prefer Boolean query models.

items.prompt: Hypothetical: an SEO wants Google results containing the exact phrase emergency boiler repair, leaving out pages with the word jobs. Which query matches Google Search Help?
options: A. "emergency boiler repair" -jobs
B. emergency boiler repair NOT jobs
C. emergency boiler repair -jobs only
D. emergency AND boiler AND repair -jobs
items.explanation: Correct: Google Search Help says to enter a phrase inside quotes for an exact match and to enter - in front of a word you want to leave out. Wrong: the saved help page doesn't list NOT, AND or 'only' as Google operators (absence in the saved page), and without quotes the phrase isn't matched exactly.

items.prompt: Hypothetical site audit plan: (1) search site:example.com to see pages from the domain; (2) search site: example.com, with a space after the colon; (3) search "returns policy" in quotes for the exact phrase; (4) search filetype:pdf to find PDFs. Which step breaks Google Search Help's guidance?
options: A. Step 1, site: followed by the domain
B. Step 2, the space after site:
C. Step 3, the phrase in quotes
D. Step 4, the filetype: search
items.explanation: Correct: Google says not to put spaces between the operator and your search term, so site: example.com won't work. Wrong: site: in front of a domain, a phrase inside quotes and filetype: in front of a file type are all described on the page.

items.prompt: Hypothetical research team, Site L. Symptom: a query of many terms joined by AND returns only 3 documents, though the team knows dozens of relevant ones exist. Evidence: (1) the textbook says using AND operators tends to produce high precision but low recall searches; (2) it defines recall as the fraction of the relevant documents in the collection that were returned; (3) it says OR gives low precision but high recall. Which diagnosis fits?
options: A. Precision is low: most of the 3 are irrelevant
B. Recall is high: the search returned most relevant documents
C. The collection holds no relevant documents
D. Recall is low: AND left relevant documents out
items.explanation: Correct: AND tends to produce low recall, and returning 3 of dozens of relevant documents is a small fraction of the relevant documents returned. Wrong: AND tends towards high, not low, precision; recall here is low, not high; the team knows relevant documents exist.

items.prompt: Hypothetical legal researcher, Site M. Symptom: after changing every AND to OR, the query returns 40,000 matches. Evidence: (1) the textbook says a document either matches or does not match a Boolean query; (2) it says the number of matching documents can far exceed the number a human user could possibly sift through; (3) it says OR gives low precision but high recall; (4) it says a satisfactory middle ground is difficult or impossible to find. What best explains the result?
options: A. OR widened recall; ranking would help sift
B. OR raised precision, so all 40,000 are relevant
C. OR cut recall, so key documents went missing
D. Boolean always finds the middle ground on its own
items.explanation: Correct: OR gives high recall and low precision, and Boolean matching gives an unranked set that can far exceed what a person can sift through, which is the textbook's case for ranked retrieval. Wrong: OR lowers precision; OR raises recall; the textbook says a satisfactory middle ground is difficult or impossible to find.
